item.title: Strategy CF: Barbell: Shaanxi Coal and the Nasdaq-100
item.description: A barbell: a coal stock on one end, the Nasdaq-100 on the other. The two tend to peak at different times. One rule in force nudges the coal position inside a ±10% band. On paper, a three-zone version sets the pair at 90/10, 60/40 or 30/70 by the rank, and three more legs sit on top: a margin add to the Nasdaq-100 when VIX closes above 30, a one-day buy when the ETF gaps down 3%, and, since Nov 4, a 63-day margin buy on the first VIX close above 20 after a calm month.

item.title: Factor F4: Volatility lights, live
item.description: Five of the six lights in the account's volatility-alert rule, measured while the market trades. They flag rough stretches; they do not call tops. When three or more are on at once, the rule says risk comes down. Refreshed every 15 minutes during US trading hours.

item.title: Factor F5: Turbulence gauge
item.description: How rough the next three months of the Nasdaq-100 are likely to be. It does not call direction or tops: it reads the Nasdaq volatility index and five lights, and puts the market in one of four tiers.

item.title: How Long Is China's Housing Cycle, and When Does It Turn?
item.description: Before 2021, China's home prices turned roughly every three years. Since the July 2021 peak they have fallen for more than five. If everything has a cycle, how long is this one, and where is the next turn? This note answers with the record of 18 housing busts since 1985, the timing of Japan's and Korea's, and four tools from mathematics and probability: a spectrum, a forecast band, an ensemble and a survival curve. The answer is a distribution, not a date.

item.title: Japan's 30 Years After the Bubble: Where Is China Now?
item.description: Three days ago we showed that 2021 broke China's housing market: before it, a city whose prices had fallen for a year usually saw them rise over the next; since then, almost never. This note asks the next question. Japan is the case everyone reaches for. How far into Japan's 30 years is China, and what does the record of housing busts say about the next five?

item.title: What Happened in 2021
item.description: Before 2021, a fall in Chinese home prices was usually temporary. Across the 70 cities in the official price survey, when a city's second-hand prices had fallen over the previous 12 months, they rose over the next 12 months 71% of the time in 2011–2020. Since 2021, that has happened 1% of the time. This note shows where the break happened, what it does to the signals people use to call a bottom, and where the 2026 rebound in Shanghai stands.

item.title: The Market Prices a 5% Chance of $140 Oil. We Think That Is Too Low.
item.description: WTI settled at $103.44 on October 23. After inflation, $140 oil is roughly where the market spent much of 2011–14, not a fantasy number. The spare capacity that capped earlier spikes is thinner than it was before the war, and inventories are falling. The futures curve still says $81 a year from now. This note sets out why we think the upside tail is underpriced, what the market itself is pricing, the evidence that cuts against us, and what would prove us wrong.
